overview: The surviving file text is a one-page “List of Papers” indexing two communications concerning Japanese telegraph regulation and censorship. The first records a French Cable Company telegram about Japan’s objection to forwarding inadequately addressed messages and a proposal that such messages be accepted only at the sender’s risk. The second records Joseph C. Grew’s report that Imperial Japanese Telegraphs, after taking over the Great Northern Telegraph Company’s business, would cease accepting messages for China proper after January 1, 1941; the underlying communications themselves are not present in the supplied OCR.

people.name: Joseph C. Grew
people.role: U.S. Ambassador to Japan; sender of telegram no. 1385 from Japan

subfiles.title: List of Papers on Japanese Telegraph Laws and Censorship
subfiles.about: An index summarizes two communications about inadequately addressed telegrams to Japan and Japanese control of cable traffic destined for China.
subfiles.summary: The first indexed item, dated September 14 under a 1939 date heading, is a telegram from the French Cable Company in New York conveying the International Telegraph Bureau at Bern’s account of a Japanese complaint about telegrams with insufficient addresses. It proposes that administrations accept such messages only at the sender’s risk. The second item is Grew’s telegram no. 1385 of December 28, reporting that Imperial Japanese Telegraphs had taken over the Great Northern Telegraph Company’s business and would stop accepting cable messages for China proper after January 1, 1941. Although the printed heading appears to assign 1939 to the dates, the 1941 effective date strongly suggests that the second entry belongs to December 1940; it is cross-referenced to file 119.2/3528.

interest: This index provides compact evidence of two distinct aspects of Japanese communications control: the practical international problem of delivering poorly addressed telegrams and the consolidation of cable traffic under Imperial Japanese Telegraphs. The second entry is especially useful for tracing the displacement of the Great Northern Telegraph Company and the restriction of communications with China at the opening of 1941. The apparent mismatch between the 1939 date heading and the second item’s 1941 effective date also highlights a cataloguing or OCR ambiguity that should be checked against the original sheet and the cited cross-reference file.
